drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: A retailer's support agent has thirty-one tools
drills.answer_line: SAM: So the answer is A.
drills.stem: A support agent has 31 tools from five teams. Three overlap (search_orders, find_order, lookup_customer_orders), each with a one-line description. The agent often calls the wrong one and returns another customer's orders. What is the best fix?

options.A: Consolidate the overlapping tools into one, with a service prefix and a detailed description of what it does, when to use it and what it returns
options.B: Add a system-prompt section listing which tool to use for which kind of question
options.C: Move the agent to the largest model
options.D: Force the agent to call the same order tool on every turn

drills.why: Overlap means consolidate; thin descriptions mean rewrite them. B works around the root cause, C is scale, D forces a tool on turns that need none.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A finance operations agent
drills.answer_line: SAM: Both. A puts the gate in code
drills.stem: Choose two. An agent reads invoices and issues payments through an internal payments API. No payment may go out without human sign-off, and invoice lookups must not interrupt the user. Which two design choices meet the policy?

options.A: Payment as a client tool the harness executes only after a human approves the specific call
options.B: Let the invoice-reading tools run without an approval step
options.C: Tell Claude in the system prompt to ask before paying
options.D: Implement payment as a server tool so Anthropic executes it securely
options.E: Require human approval for every tool call, reads included

drills.why: Gate the irreversible action in code; leave reads alone. C is a polite instruction, D is impossible (server tools are Anthropic's), E breaks "must not interrupt".

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. For each item, say tool, resource or prompt.
drills.answer_line: SAM: All four. Four is a tool
drills.prompt: Tool, resource or prompt? (1) A database schema the app attaches as read-only context. (2) A create-incident action Claude decides to call. (3) A "triage this incident" template a user picks from the slash menu. (4) A run-query operation that takes SQL and returns rows.
drills.answer: (1) Resource. (2) Tool. (3) Prompt. (4) Tool: Claude invokes it with arguments and it executes, even though it only reads.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A developer's local stdio M C P server
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. Send logs to standard error
drills.stem: A local stdio MCP server worked in testing. After the developer added print statements to debug a tool, Claude Code reports it cannot talk to the server. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Print writes to stdout, corrupting the JSON-RPC messages; log to stderr instead
options.B: stdio is unreliable, so the server must move to Streamable HTTP
options.C: The tool descriptions became too long for the client
options.D: The model in use does not support MCP

drills.why: In a stdio server, stdout carries the protocol. "Worked until" names the cause; B rebuilds the deployment around a one-line bug.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. An insurer's claims assistant
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. Know-how, needed only sometimes
drills.stem: A claims assistant should follow a ten-step fraud-referral procedure, with a scoring table and a small calculation script, only on claims that hit a red flag. Nothing external needs connecting. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Package the procedure, table and script as a Skill that loads when a claim matches
options.B: Build an MCP server that exposes the procedure as a tool
options.C: Paste the procedure and table into the system prompt
options.D: Write one custom tool for each of the ten steps

drills.why: Know-how needed only sometimes, with a bundled script: a Skill. B is connectivity nobody needs, C pays on every claim, D crowds the tool set.

drills.question_line: SAM: Recall first. Pause and name the three skills from today
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Tool implementation: who runs the call
drills.prompt: Name the three skills from today, and the question that sorts each one.
drills.answer: Tool implementation (who runs the call, what it says on failure); MCP development (tool, resource or prompt; local or remote); customization (does it exist, who needs it, access or know-how).

In this episode: Trace the tool-use loop and who executes each tool
Descriptions and error results that keep an agent on track
Build an MCP server: transport, tools, resources, prompts
Choose built-in, custom tool, Skill or MCP
Cold open: the wrong lookup: Three overlapping order tools, one-line descriptions each
Wrong tool called: another customer's order history
Consolidate, route in the prompt, scale up, or force one tool?
Tool implementation: stop_reason tool_use → harness dispatches by name → tool_result with the same ID
Tool runner in the SDK runs the loop for you
Client tools run in your app; server tools run on Anthropic's side
Tool set construction: size, naming, what each tool returns
Errors: is_error true with what failed and what to try next
The model proposes a call; the harness decides whether it runs
MCP server development: Host creates one MCP client per server; messages are JSON-RPC
Tools model-controlled, resources app-controlled, prompts user-controlled
stdio: local process launched by the client
Streamable HTTP: remote service, many clients, OAuth recommended
Python SDK builds tool definitions from type hints and docstrings
Claude Code .mcp.json, Claude Desktop, and the API's MCP connector
Agentic customization: Q1: does a built-in tool already do it?
Q2: an action for one application → custom tool in its code
Q3: shared access across apps, maintained independently → MCP
Q4: know-how rather than access → consider progressive loading
MCP gives access; know-how says how to use it
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: A, consolidate with a detailed, prefixed description
B: a routing table works around thin descriptions
C: scale instead of a fix
D: forces a tool on turns that need none
Tell: "three of them overlap" and "a one-line description"
Five to remember: Loop: tool_use → dispatch → tool_result; client vs server tools
Descriptions are the top factor; fewer tools, prefixes, lean returns
Instructive is_error results; approval gates on irreversible actions
MCP: tools/resources/prompts by controller; stdio local, HTTP remote
Built-in if it exists; custom for one app; MCP shared; Skill for know-how
Recap: the exam tells: Wrong one of several similar tools → consolidate and rewrite descriptions
Agent invents an answer when a tool fails → instructive is_error result
Payment, delete or send → approval gate in the harness on that tool
Read-only context the app attaches → resource; menu template → prompt
stdio server broke after prints → stdout; log to stderr
Many clients over a network → Streamable HTTP
Several apps need the same access → MCP; one app → custom tool
